challenges.name: hashed-refresh-tokens-quiz
challenges.title: What a hashed token store protects
challenges.description: Two pieces of evidence from the leaked-backup incident: a review comment that asks for bcrypt, and an attacker replaying a value copied from the backup.

questions.explanation: False. A slow, salted hash protects secrets that people choose, because those have little entropy and can be guessed from a dictionary. This token is 32 bytes from a cryptographic random generator: 256 bits, so there is no dictionary and an exhaustive search is out of reach even at billions of SHA-256 per second. bcrypt would also break the design: its salt makes the same token hash differently each time, so the server could no longer find the row with WHERE token_hash = $1 and would have to bcrypt-compare against every row, at about 0.25 s each. The misconception is that "fast hash" is a weakness by itself; it is a weakness only for low-entropy secrets such as passwords. OWASP's Password Storage Cheat Sheet is about passwords, not about random tokens.

questions.question:
After the fix, someone replays a value taken from the leaked backup (row rt_1842 of user u_ana):

$ curl -s -X POST https://api.codedev.test/auth/refresh \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d '{"refreshToken":"9f2c4e0b7a1d...e85a"}'      # 64 hex characters: the token_hash column of rt_1842
{"error":"invalid_grant"}

API log: refresh_token.rejected reason=malformed

The server's validate code checks the format (43 base64url characters), then runs SHA-256 over what it received and looks up WHERE token_hash = $1.

Statement: "Even if the format check were removed, this replay would fail, because the server would hash the 64 hex characters and SHA-256 of a hash matches no token_hash in the table."
questions.explanation: True. The table stores H(token) and the server always computes H(presented). Presenting H(token) makes the server look up H(H(token)), which is not in the table, so the lookup finds nothing and the result is "unknown". That is the whole point of storing hashes: what is at rest is not what a client sends. The format check is a cheap early rejection and keeps junk out of the logs and the database, but security does not depend on it. The misconception is that a stolen hash can be "passed through" like a password hash in a pass-the-hash attack; that only works when the server accepts the hash itself as the credential.

challenges.name: store-refresh-tokens-as-hashes
challenges.title: Store refresh tokens as hashes
challenges.description:
A copy of the CodeDev auth database leaked from a backup bucket, and the refresh tokens in it still worked: the table stored them in plain text. Write the two functions of the new token store so that the table only ever holds SHA-256 hashes.

issueRefreshToken(deps, userId, deviceId): create the token from deps.randomBytes(32).toString("base64url") (43 characters). Take id = deps.newId("rt") and then familyId = deps.newId("fam") (every issue starts a new family here). Insert one row with deps.store.insert: tokenHash = SHA-256 of the token as lowercase hex, createdAt = deps.now(), expiresAt = createdAt + deps.ttlMs, usedAt, revokedAt and replacedBy null. Log { event: "refresh_token.issued", id, userId, deviceId } and return { token, id, familyId, expiresAt }.

validateRefreshToken(deps, presented): presented comes straight from the request body and may be anything. Check in this order and return the first match: (1) not a string of exactly 43 characters from A-Z a-z 0-9 - _ -> { ok: false, reason: "malformed" } without touching the store; (2) hash it and call deps.store.findByHash(hash); no row, or a row whose tokenHash is not equal to the hash (compare the bytes with crypto.timingSafeEqual) -> "unknown"; (3) row.revokedAt is not null -> "revoked"; (4) deps.now() >= row.expiresAt -> "expired"; (5) otherwise { ok: true, id, familyId, userId, deviceId, expiresAt } of the row. Every rejection logs { event: "refresh_token.rejected", reason } with an id property added when a row was found (revoked, expired); a success logs { event: "refresh_token.accepted", id }. Log each event with these properties in this order.

A token or a stored hash must never appear in the store as plain text, in a log event or in a validate result. The test runner prints every operation with its log events, then the store (tokenHash shown as sha256(#n) when it is the hash of the n-th issued token, PLAIN(#n) when it is the token itself) and a leak check over the store, the logs and the results. Do not change the types, the store or the runner.
hints: What exactly must the database hold so that a server can still recognise a token it issued, while a copy of the database gives an attacker nothing to send?

Look at three places: what you pass to store.insert (only tokenHash, never the token), the order of the checks in validate (format, lookup, revoked, expired), and every object you pass to deps.log or return from validate - none of them may carry the token or row.tokenHash.

A similar case with API keys: key = randomBytes(24).toString("base64url") gives 32 characters; the table keeps createHash("sha256").update(key).digest("hex"). To check a key, hash what the client sent, look up that hash, then compare Buffer.from(row.keyHash, "hex") with Buffer.from(hash, "hex") using timingSafeEqual (both 32 bytes). A key that was disabled yesterday is rejected as disabled before anyone looks at its expiry.

tests.name: Two devices sign in; both tokens validate and only their SHA-256 hashes are stored
Revoked, expired and unknown tokens are rejected with their reason and logged without secrets
The backup replay: a tokenHash value presented as a token is rejected, the real token still works
Expiry boundary with a 15-minute TTL: valid 1 ms before expiresAt, expired at expiresAt
Same user and device sign in twice: two families, two hashes; revoked wins over expired
Invalid input: null, number, object, empty, bad length, padding, +/ are malformed; forged is unknown
Large: 290 tokens for 30 users and 8 devices, 20 revoked, 616 checks over 31 days

issued: 290
validate expired: 220
validate malformed: 6
validate ok: 370
validate revoked: 20
store:
290 rows, 290 with tokenHash = sha256(token), 20 revoked
leaks: none
